name: PT Nusantara Sejahtera Raya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Cinema XXI: the national exhibitor priced for a fade
frontmatter.summary: Indonesia's dominant cinema chain is priced for a secular decline: nine-month profit fell 6.4% on a weak slate and the shares sit at 3.5x forward EV/EBITDA. But the third quarter grew revenue 7.5% year-on-year, the estate is the only national footprint at 1,402 screens, and free cash flow covers a distribution above profit. The price implies revenue shrinking -4.3% a year; we think 3.0% nominal is likelier. BUY, target Rp145.
thesis: The footprint is the moat and the policy tailwind: 1,402 screens screens across 55 cities and 31 regencies is the only national chain, and the Ministry of Culture's target of 10,000 screens national screens against about 2,500 today implies category expansion rather than contraction [S3, S7].

The earnings are cash: tickets are paid at the counter and through TIX ID and GoPay before supplier terms fall due, so working capital is negative, D&A exceeds capex, and the company distributed more than its FY2025 attributable profit without adding debt [S0, S11].

The price already assumes the bear case: the reverse DCF reads -4.3% revenue growth out of Rp74, against a base case of 3.0%-3.5% and a bear case that still values the shares above today's price [S0].

catalysts.event: Payment of the interim dividend declared 31 October 2026
FY2026 results: fourth-quarter slate and the first read on 2027 admissions
Annual meeting and FY2026 final dividend decision

blocks.text: BUY, target Rp145, 109.0% total return from Rp74 [S0]. The company is PT Nusantara Sejahtera Raya Tbk, which trades as Cinema XXI and operates the largest cinema circuit in Indonesia: 271 locations and 1,402 screens across 55 cities and 31 regencies at the end of October 2026 [S3, F19, F20]. Nine-month 2026 revenue of IDR4.20tn produced net profit of IDR416.3bn and EBITDA of IDR1.20tn, an EBITDA margin on a revenue line that was smaller than the same nine months of 2025 [S3, S9, F1, F10].

The variant view is about duration, not direction. We accept the direction: revenue grew 2.6% in FY2025 to Rp5,860.4bn and is down about a point in FY2026, and the first half of 2026 was genuinely weak [S5, S9]. What we do not accept is that the weakness is permanent. The third quarter alone grew revenue 7.5% year on year, food-and-beverage revenue grew 13.9% and average spend per patron rose 15.8%, with the average ticket price up 2.0% on premium-format occupancy [S9, F26, F27, F28]. A business whose quarterly revenue can re-accelerate to 7.5% while holding an EBITDA margin near thirty per cent is not in structural run-off; it is in a flat-to-low-growth phase with a film-slate cycle on top.

The price disagrees. At Rp74 the shares trade at 3.5x forward EV/EBITDA and 9.5x forward earnings, with the dividend yield at 13.1% on the Rp10 per share we expect over the next twelve months [S0]. The reverse DCF says that price requires revenue to shrink -4.3% a year across the explicit forecast. That is the bear case applied to the whole horizon, not a central expectation.

Three things move the value. First, the revenue-growth path: one point of growth is worth several rupiah per share at this WACC. Second, the terminal rate, where we have taken 3.3% against a higher house default because the group's own growth has decelerated for three years [S5, S9] - a rate still above the zero the price implies. Third, the distribution policy: the company pays out more than it earns because D&A exceeds capex, and at a 13.1% forward yield the cash return does most of the work in the total return even if the multiple never re-rates [S0, S11].

Cinema XXI sells three things on the same asset base: a seat in a dark room, food and drink consumed in it, and the attention of the people sitting there. That is the whole business, and it is why the segment mix matters more than the location count. For the nine months to September 2026, ticket sales contributed IDR2.50tn, or 59.1% of revenue; food and beverage contributed IDR1.40tn, or 34.7%; and advertising, digital platform and other services contributed 6.5% of revenue - up from a much smaller share a year earlier [S3, F13, F15, F17]. The third stream is small but the fastest-growing: the company itself attributes the shift to advertising and its digital platform alongside the two core lines [S3].

The estate is the asset. At 29 October 2026 the circuit stood at 271 locations and 1,402 screens across 55 cities and 31 regencies, after opening four locations and 14.0 screens screens during 2026: Ciplaz Cipanas, Semarang, Grand Mall Maros and Sorong Modern City [S3, F19, F20, F21]. That is about one per cent screen growth in a year, a deliberate step-down from the post-IPO build. The geography is the point: a circuit that reaches regency towns as well as the Jakarta premium market is buying the only defensible position in a business where the constraint is physical - a rival cannot stream its way into Sorong.

Revenue per screen is the operating metric the model leans on. FY2025 revenue of Rp5,860.4bn across the estate is in the order of a few billion rupiah per screen per year, and the third quarter of 2026 improved on that base through mix rather than price: average ticket price rose 2.0% but food-and-beverage spend per patron rose 15.8% [S9, F26, F28]. That mix shift is the most encouraging operating datum in the file, because it comes from the counter, not from the box office, and it is not slate-dependent.

Strategy, as management states it, is to keep the core strong while developing other revenue lines and to expand selectively into areas it judges promising [S3]. The affordability commitment is explicit: the president director says the company tries to minimise ticket price increases so the cinema stays accessible to all income groups [S3]. We read that as a share-defence strategy rather than a margin strategy, and it is confirmed by the 2.0% average ticket price growth in a year when input costs ran at headline inflation [S9, F26].

Group structure. The company is a subsidiary of PT Harkatjaya Bumipersada [S0]. The listed entity is 93.2% held by insiders with a free float of 8.1%, which is the single most important structural fact about the shares and is covered in the governance section [S0]. Cinema XXI is the leader, not a challenger: no other circuit in the country operates a comparable national footprint, and the four openings in 2026 were all in under-screened secondary towns rather than in a defended Jakarta core [S3, F21].

The industry is small, physically constrained and politically favoured. The Ministry of Culture set a target on 11 November 2026 to add screens until the country reaches 10,000 screens screens from about 2,500 operating today, describing the constraint on national film as a shortage of playing space rather than a shortage of production, and calling for regional investment rather than limits on output [S7, F29, F37]. Cinema XXI's 1,402 screens screens are therefore above half of the national base - the single strongest structural fact in the file, because it means the incumbent already owns the distribution that the policy is trying to expand. The target cuts both ways: it supports category expansion, but the ministry explicitly invites independent and mini-cinema investors into the regions, which over a decade is share dilution rather than share gain for the listed circuit [S7]. We treat it as a tailwind that raises the probability of continued category expansion, not as a number in the model.

The demand side is now measurable. Admissions were 80.3 million in 2025 against 80.2 million in 2024 - essentially flat while the number of Indonesian films released rose by about two-fifths [S7, F33, F34] - and the same industry data put attendance at 47.8 million to October 2026 against a full-year projection of about 59 million, a fall of roughly a quarter [S7, F35, F36]. Admissions per local title fell from 553 thousand in 2024 to 399 thousand in 2025 [S7, F38, F39]. That is the strongest evidence for the bear case in the source set: volume has been flat at best since 2024 and is now falling, so any growth has to come from ticket price, F&B attach and screen count. Our base case carries exactly that mix, and the bear case tests the volume line breaking further.

The demand driver is discretionary spending, and the macro deck is explicitly against us. Indonesian real GDP is put at 5.3 rate% with CPI at 3.3 rate% and the policy rate at 5.8 rate%, and the house tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer discretionary is AVOID within the balance-of-payments-pressure regime [S12]. We do not soften that: we state it and argue the exemption. Cinema XXI has no floating-rate debt of consequence and no consumer credit book, so the policy rate does not reach its interest line; its leases are long-dated fixed contracts, so the rate channel into occupancy cost is slow; and its average ticket is at the affordable end of the discretionary basket, which is a defence in a squeeze rather than an offset to one [S0, S3]. The tilt is carried in the multiple and in the bear case, not in the base-case growth rate.

Globally, exhibition is a mature business in which the number of screens grows slowly, attendance
is driven by the strength of the release slate, and the exhibitor keeps a minority of the ticket
price while keeping most of the concession margin. Those mechanics are general to the format rather
than specific to this issuer, and are flagged here as unverified context rather than as sourced fact.

Competitive structure. Rivalry is concentrated at the top: one national circuit, a Korean-backed chain and a long tail of single-location operators. New entry is capital-intensive and gated by mall relationships, so the realistic threat is a rival expanding in the same malls rather than a new national entrant. Substitution is the real force, and it is the one the market is pricing: streaming and short-form video compete for the same evening, and the evidence of that competition is in the industry attendance series and in the company's own revenue line - growth of 2.6% in FY2025 and a decline in the first nine months of 2026 [S5, S7, S9]. Supplier power sits with film distributors, who take a rental share of the ticket; buyer power is negligible because the customer is an atomised walk-up purchaser.

The moat is distribution density plus format. A circuit of this size negotiates film-rental terms and mall leases from strength, and premium formats - The Premiere and IMAX - carry a higher ticket price and were cited as the reason average ticket price rose 2.0% in the third quarter even as attendance was soft [S9, F26]. Distribution reach into 31 regencies is the part a new entrant cannot buy quickly. What the moat does not do is protect the category from substitution, and we do not claim it does: the base case grows revenue at 3.0% to 3.5%, roughly flat in real terms, which is a share-defence assumption rather than a share-gain one [S9, S12].

The five-forces read is therefore: high substitute pressure, moderate rivalry, low buyer power, moderate supplier power, moderate entry barriers [S3, S5, S9]. That configuration supports a business that earns a return above its cost of capital on a flat volume base - which is precisely how the model is built - but it does not support a re-rating to growth multiples, and the valuation does not assume one.

The five-year record is a recovery that ran out of momentum. Revenue went from Rp4,401.1bn in FY2022 to Rp5,230.8bn, Rp5,711.8bn and Rp5,860.4bn, which is growth of 2.6% in the last year against 9.2% the year before [S0, S5, F8]. The pattern is the familiar one for an exhibition business coming out of a closure: a sharp recovery, then a plateau set by the size of the estate and the strength of the release slate. EBITDA followed the same shape, from Rp1,747.4bn to Rp1,846.1bn, with the margin at 31.5% in FY2025 [S0].

FY2026 is the year the plateau turned down. Nine-month revenue of IDR4.20tn is below the IDR4.30tn of the prior-year nine months - a fall of about two per cent, not the three and a half the FY2025 total scaled by nine twelfths would suggest, because the fourth quarter is the seasonally strongest - and net profit of IDR416.3bn is 6.4% lower than the IDR444.9bn booked a year earlier [S3, S9, F1, F10, F11, F12]. The decline is not uniform: the first half was weak and the third quarter grew revenue 7.5% year on year [S9, F18]. For the full year we therefore carry revenue of Rp5,790.1bn, a -1.2% change, which implies fourth-quarter revenue about two per cent above the year-earlier quarter, with an EBITDA margin of 29.9% and an EBIT margin of 16.5% [S0]. That EBIT margin is below the 17.9% realised in FY2025, and the gap is the honest part of this model: the nine-month cost base did not shrink with revenue, and 2026 pays for a weaker slate.

The revenue build is one line, because the company reports one consolidated revenue line in the periodic releases, and the segment split is disclosed only by activity in percentage terms [S3, F14, F16, F17]. Growth from FY2027 is 3.0% rising to 3.5%, which is admissions roughly flat and price/mix carrying the rest. The assumption is anchored on the 2.0% average ticket price growth and the 15.8% food-and-beverage spend-per-patron growth the company reported in the third quarter [S9] - mix, not price, is doing the work, and that is the part of the model we are most comfortable defending.

Costs and margins. The gross margin was 60.1% of revenue in FY2025 - cost of revenue of IDR2,336.1bn on revenue of IDR5,860.4bn, and the cost line includes film rental, concession cost and the direct cost of the F&B operation [S0]. The model holds the gross margin at 59.4% in FY2026E and 59.7% thereafter, a slight compression from the FY2025 realised level on the evidence of a nine-month period in which revenue fell while film-rental and input costs did not [S3]. SG&A is 42.9% of revenue in FY2026E, above the 2,473.8/revenue ratio of the last actual, for the same reason, and eases as the revenue base grows against a fixed screen cost base [S0].

Cash flow is where this business is better than its earnings. Depreciation and amortisation of Rp795.6bn exceeds capex of Rp656.6bn, so free cash flow of Rp997.5bn exceeds net profit of Rp776.2bn [S0]. Three things do this: the estate is past its heaviest build, the leased and owned assets are long-lived, and working capital is negative. The nine-month operating cash flow of IDR931.4bn against net profit of IDR416.3bn is the cleanest evidence in the file that the reported earnings are cash-backed [S3, F2, F4].

Working capital. Tickets are paid at the counter, at the kiosk or through TIX ID and GoPay, and supplier terms on film rental and F&B stock run a month or more, so the operating working capital position is a source of cash rather than a use: minus Rp-394.0bn at FY2025, or about -7.0% of revenue [S0]. The model carries that structure forward, which is why the free cash flow conversion stays above one even as revenue growth slows. It also means the business needs little incremental funding to grow one per cent of screens a year.

Balance sheet and debt. The last balance sheet is the 30 June 2026 interim, not the FY2025 year-end: at that date it held cash of about one point four trillion rupiah against debt of about one point six five trillion, a net DEBT position of roughly a quarter of a trillion [S0]. The FY2025 year-end, by contrast, showed net cash of -132.3bn [S0], and the difference is explained by the cash calendar rather than by a change in policy: the seven rupiah per share FY2025 final absorbed IDR583.0bn in April 2026 [S0, F24], minority dividends of IDR89.4bn were paid, and the half year carries the weaker slate and the lower seasonal revenue, while the fourth quarter is the strongest of the year. The model therefore closes FY2026E at a net cash position of -292.3bn [S0] only because the engine books a year's dividend on the prior year's DPS: the IDR333.1bn interim declared on 31 October 2026 [S6, F23] sits in the following year's cash line, and on the actual June position the company is modestly levered, not in net cash. Some of that debt is likely lease liability under the accounting standard for leases rather than bank borrowing; the LK note that would split it is not in the source set, and we flag that as an open item rather than guess. Equity of Rp4,136.5bn against net profit gives a return on equity of 16.5%, which is the number that matters for a company with a 1.5x price-to-book: the market is paying close to book for a mid-teens return on equity [S0].

Capital allocation. The company distributes more than it earns. The FY2025 annual meeting approved Rp12.0/share per share, IDR980.0bn in total, against attributable profit of Rp704.8bn [S11, F24, F25, S0] - about one and four tenths of attributable profit on the single definition we use throughout this report, declared DPS over attributable EPS, which is the ratio in section six as well. The cash actually paid in a calendar year differs from the declared figure because the final is paid in April and the interim in November: the datapack's cash dividend line of Rp821.1bn for FY2025 is that cash-paid basis, and it is the lagged number, not a second measure of the same year's policy. That the distribution exceeds profit is possible because free cash flow of IDR997.5bn exceeds net profit, and it is the clearest statement of management's priorities: no debt reduction, no large acquisition, cash back to shareholders. The same meeting approved the distribution of treasury shares to shareholders in proportion to their holdings, which is a capital return in kind rather than a buyback funded from the market [S11]. We do not value it separately: the number of treasury shares is not disclosed in the registered sources, so a per-share value cannot be computed, and the effect is to transfer existing shares rather than to create value at the group level.

Earnings-quality flags, run against the house card. The accruals ratio is negative, not positive: cash flow runs well ahead of net profit in every period examined [S0, S3]. Receivables are not growing faster than revenue because there are effectively no trade receivables - the customer pays before the lights go down - and inventory is food stock, not a build. The IDX regime is clean: no special monitoring board and no special notation is disclosed in the datapack or press coverage [S0]. Related-party exposure appears limited to the parent relationship, with no disclosed material sales to or purchases from affiliates in the period covered, though the LK's related- party note could not be archived and this is a gap rather than an all-clear [S0]. Structure flags are real but disclosed: a 93.2% insider holding with a 8.1% free float, and a treasury-share distribution that returns capital without a cash buyback [S0, S11]. None of these is manipulation-class on the evidence available; the float is an optics-class flag that we carry explicitly in the valuation rather than bury in a discount.

An exhibitor is a cash-flow asset, not a growth option. It owns long-lived fit-outs and lease interests, its revenue is a function of seats and price rather than of a reinvestment programme, and its terminal economics depend on whether people keep going to the cinema. A discounted cash flow is the right primary method for that shape. It is also the method that lets us separate the two questions the market is conflating - will admissions fall, and what is a flat admission worth - because the second is a discount-rate and terminal-growth question while the first is a revenue question, and only the DCF keeps them apart.

The compounder card asks for the growth arithmetic. Reinvestment is not the constraint here. Capex of 11.5% of revenue runs below D&A of 13.4%, so the reinvestment rate is negative in the sense that the company recovers more capital than it spends to hold the estate; growth of 3.0% therefore comes from ticket price and F&B attach on assets already in place, not from capital deployed. The return on that existing capital is 15.5% on book equity, well above the 11.9% cost of capital, which is what makes a no-growth business worth more than book. Because there is no reinvestment engine, the ROIIC question is not meaningful in the usual form: we do not need heroic incremental returns to justify the growth, and equally we should not pay for growth we cannot see in capex. That is why the target sits near the DCF value rather than at a growth premium.

The WACC of 11.9% is inside the house IDR band and the build is fully disclosed. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, from which the engine deducts a default spread of 1.6% to reach the sovereign-free rate it uses in the cost of equity. On top sit a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, applied to an unlevered beta of 0.90 - the industry default, not a company regression, because the shares have too short and too illiquid a history to estimate one - relevered at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.27 to 1.09, with the tax shield at 22.0% [S0]. The cost of equity is therefore 13.1%; the pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4%; and with weights of 78.9% equity to 21.1% debt the WACC is 11.9%. We have not applied a liquidity discount: the three-month average daily traded value is comfortably above the fund's lowest liquidity tier, and a discount would be a hidden haircut rather than a modelled fact [S0].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of 11,415.1 against FY2026E EBITDA of Rp1,733.3bn and a terminal-value share of 45.3% [weight 90%] [S0]. A terminal share below half is the test of whether a DCF is really a terminal-value story in disguise: this one is not, because the explicit period carries the majority of the value. The bridge from enterprise to equity value is explicit: net debt at the 30 June 2026 balance sheet - a small net debt position, not the year-end net cash the model's own cash line closes on - is deducted, minorities of IDR174.6bn are deducted, and there are no investments or other bridge items, which gives the Rp132 per share the method contributes [S0]. Terminal growth is 3.3%, the macro deck's long-run CPI for Indonesia [S12], so the terminal rate is zero in real terms: it assumes the cinema share of consumer spend holds and no more, which is materially below the nominal GDP the geography implies and below the 11.9% WACC as a perpetuity rate must be [S12, S0].

The multiple-survival test. A DCF is a hidden re-rating when the terminal value assumes an exit multiple above the entry multiple. Here it does not, but the expansion is real and we state it: the terminal value is roughly six times terminal-year EBITDA and about eleven times terminal-year EBIT, on FY2035E EBITDA of Rp2,340.6bn and EBIT of Rp1,310.8bn [S0]. At entry the shares are on 3.4x FY2025 EV/EBITDA, so the terminal multiple is a substantial expansion on the price paid - of the order of three quarters - and it is not a modest fade-and-exit; but it is below the 7.3 peer median the engine carries and below the shares' own three-year mean of about nine times, which is the standard the market itself applied to this business before the de-rating [S0]. An exit at six times is rational if the business is still earning a mid-teens return on equity on a flat volume base in ten years: that is a claim about the terminal economics, not about growth, and it is the claim the whole file rests on. The only like-for-like multiple available is the EV/EBITDA cross-check at 7.3, which sits 18.0% above the primary method. That peer median is drawn from Indonesian hospitality and villa names, not from cinema exhibitors, and we weight it at 10% as a ceiling check rather than as a value. We do not use a P/E cross-check at all: the engine's peer P/E median is a hospitality number, and applying it to this earnings stream would be multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume. Weights are therefore 90% DCF to 10% multiple, as set in the assumptions.

What the price implies. The reverse DCF reads -4.3% revenue growth in FY2027E at the current Rp74 price [S0]. That is the market telling us it expects the weak first half of 2026 to be the permanent run-rate, with no recovery in the slate and no benefit from the screen-expansion policy. Our base case assumes 3.0% growth, which is still a de-rating of the category relative to nominal GDP; the bear case subtracts three points and still values the shares above the current price, because the terminal value and the cash return do the work.

The three assumptions carrying most of the value are revenue growth, the gross margin and the WACC. A one-point change in the near-term growth rate moves the value by roughly a tenth; a hundred basis points of gross margin moves it by a similar order; a one-point change in WACC moves it by about the same. The model is not a knife-edge: the bear case is Rp106, the base Rp142 and the bull Rp189 [S0]. What that range does not do is reach the market price. We say so plainly: at Rp74 the shares are below every constructed case, and to be worth that the business would have to combine the reverse-DCF revenue path with a terminal value of close to nothing - no operating shock we can mirror produces it. That is a statement about what the price requires, not a fourth scenario, and it is the reason the position is a BUY rather than a HOLD with a wide band.
The risks that matter are demand and structure, in that order.

Substitution and slate risk is the highest-likelihood risk and the one the price already reflects. Streaming and short-form video compete for the same evening, and the company's revenue fell in the first nine months of 2026 after growing only 2.6% in FY2025 [S5, S9]. The industry attendance series says the same thing from the other side: volume was flat in 2025 and is running at roughly a quarter below that pace in 2026 [S7, F33, F35, F36]. Likelihood: high. Impact on value: this is the bear case, Rp106, roughly a quarter below the base. It is not a tail - it is the case the market is currently pricing, and the reverse DCF says so directly.

Distribution risk is new and already visible. The FY2026 interim of Rp4.0/share per share, IDR333.1bn, declared on 31 October 2026 [S6, F22, F23], is nearly a fifth below the FY2025 interim paid in November 2025 [S0]. So the payout is being cut with profit rather than held through a weak year, and the total-return case cannot assume the trailing yield persists at the declared rate - the forward yield in this file is on the Rp10 we model, which is a cut on the trailing distribution, not an extension of it. Likelihood of a further cut: medium, tied to the FY2026 result and the April 2027 meeting. Impact: high, because the distribution is the largest single component of the expected return.

Free-float compliance is a dated supply risk. The registry shows a free float of 8.1% against a fifteen per cent minimum for this board, so the shares are non-compliant today, with a twelve and a half per cent step due on 31 March 2027 - four and a half months away [S0]. A controlling shareholder can meet that by selling down or by a rights-style mechanism, and either way it is supply: a sale is an overhang into a thin market, and an issue dilutes per-share value. Likelihood: high that the threshold is tested on that date. Impact: medium on the price, low on fundamental value - which is why it sits in the risks and not in the DCF.

Leverage is small but it is not net cash. At the 30 June 2026 balance sheet the company carried net debt, having closed FY2025 in net cash of -132.3bn; the model's own closing net cash of -292.3bn reflects the engine booking the declared interim in the following year's cash line [S0, S6, F23]. The debt is roughly one year's EBITDA at most and partly lease liability, so it is not a solvency question, but a file that called this balance sheet net cash would be overstating the financial flexibility behind the payout.

Macro and consumer-spending risk is medium-likelihood and medium-impact. Cinema is discretionary, and the macro deck carries CPI at 3.3 rate with real GDP at 5.3 rate while the house tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer discretionary is AVOID [S12]. A squeeze compresses attendance before it compresses price, because the company has committed to keeping tickets affordable [S3]. The offset is that cinema is among the cheapest paid entertainment available, which limits the downside elasticity; section two sets out why the rate channel reaches this business only slowly.

Operational risk is medium-likelihood and low-to-medium impact: a weak slate is a quarterly event, not a structural one, and the third quarter of 2026 shows how quickly it reverses [S9, F18]. The estate is owned or leased on long terms, so capacity is not lost in a bad year; the cost is under-absorbed fixed cost, which is what the model carries in FY2026E.

Governance and structure risk is low-likelihood but high-impact if it materialises, and it is the one we cannot fully clear. The free float is 8.1% with 93.2% held by insiders [S0]. A company with that structure can be run for the controlling family's interests rather than for the minority's, and the treasury-share distribution approved at the FY2025 meeting is a related-party-adjacent transaction we could not examine in detail because the circular was not archived [S11]. We have no evidence of abuse; we also have no evidence of the absence of it, and we say so rather than paper over it.

Currency and commodity risk are negligible: revenue, costs and debt are all in rupiah and there is no traded input with a benchmark price [S0]. Regulatory risk is low and, if anything, positive in direction, because the Ministry of Culture wants more screens rather than fewer [S7, F29]. Price regulation is the tail: a cap on ticket prices would break the affordability-plus-mix model, but no such proposal is in the source set.

Liquidity risk is a live constraint for a fund, not for the company. The shares trade about a few billion rupiah of value a day on average, which is workable but not deep, and the 8.1% free float means a position has to be built patiently [S0]. The company's own liquidity is adequate but not lavish: it closed FY2025 in net cash and carried net debt of about a quarter of a trillion rupiah at the 30 June 2026 interim, with the distribution funded from the free cash flow that D&A above capex produces [S0, F23].

The scenarios are mirrored on the same two drivers. The bear subtracts three points of revenue growth and one and a half points of gross margin; the bull adds the same amounts, on the evidence of the third-quarter recovery and the policy tailwind [S9, S7]. Probabilities are 0.5 base, 0.2 bear and 0.2 bull, and they sum to one. We do not shock the terminal rate, the payout or capex in either direction, because those are policy choices the company has been consistent about and a scenario should test the operating business, not re-write the capital allocation.

For completeness, the case the price implies. The reverse DCF reads -4.3% revenue growth in FY2027E, and at Rp74 the market is capitalising that path with a terminal value close to nothing. To be worth the market price on our framework, revenue would have to compound down at about that rate through the forecast *and* the terminal rate would have to go to zero, with the gross margin at the bottom of its history: no mirrored operating shock reaches it, and the sensitivity grid at four points below base growth and two points below gross margin still values the shares well above the price [S0]. What the bearer of the price has to believe is not that 2026 is weak - that is our bear case - but that the cinema screen in Indonesia has no terminal value at all. We do not believe that, and the admissions series and the 1,402 screens-screen footprint are why.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of importance: a second consecutive quarter of year-on-year revenue decline would move us toward the bear case; a fourth-quarter 2026 print at or above the third quarter's growth would move us toward the bull; a distribution cut, or new debt to fund it, would break the cash-return logic and force a re-underwrite; any related-party transaction larger than a rounding error would move governance from optics to manipulation-class and, per the house card, end the position.

Ownership and control are concentrated. The company is a subsidiary of PT Harkatjaya Bumipersada, and 93.2% of the shares are held by insiders against a free float of 8.1% and an institutional holding of 3.3% [S0]. Those three figures overlap rather than add: the registry's insider block includes holders that also appear in the institutional count, which is why the sum exceeds one hundred per cent, and the float is the residual the market can actually trade. Management is the founding family: the president director, Suryo Suherman, is the public face of the company in every results statement we registered, and the board includes Arif Suherman, Dody Suhartono and Tri Rudy Anitio as directors [S11, S3]. A controlling family that runs the business is not inherently a governance problem for an operating company - it is often the opposite - but the minority's protection depends on the family's own standards, and the free float gives the market little leverage to enforce any.

Related-party dealings. No material related-party revenue or purchase is disclosed in the sources registered for this report [S0, S3]. That is a statement about the evidence, not a clean bill of health: the LK's related-party note was not archived, and the parent relationship alone - a holding company above a cash-generative subsidiary - is the channel through which value would leak if it leaked. We flag this as an open item for the next update, when the FY2026 LK will be available.

Pledged shares. The datapack carries no pledged-share disclosure for the controlling stake [S0]. Given the concentration, a pledge would be a margin-call risk on the float, and it is a specific item we would check in the annual report's shareholder section, which the IR site did not serve to the fetcher.

Auditor and opinion. Not disclosed in the registered sources; the FY2025 accounts in the datapack are the audited annual figures and the model anchors on them [S0]. There is no auditor change or qualification in the press coverage we registered. This is a gap to close at the next update.

Dividend record. The company is a consistent and generous distributor, and this is the strongest governance signal in the file. FY2025 declared Rp12.0/share per share, IDR980.0bn, or about one and four tenths of attributable profit of Rp704.8bn - the same declared-DPS over attributable-EPS measure used in section three [S11, F24, F25, S0]. The lower ratio the datapack shows is a different thing: it divides the cash actually paid in the year by that year's earnings, which mixes dividends declared out of the prior year's profit with the current year's result, and it is the reason the cash line of Rp821.1bn does not equal the declared Rp980 IDR bnbn. The FY2026 interim of Rp4.0/share per share, IDR333.1bn, was declared on 31 October 2026 with payment on 19 November [S6, F22, F23]. That interim is below the FY2025 interim, so the board has cut with profit rather than held the distribution through a down year - a disciplined signal on capital allocation and a weaker one for the total-return case than an unchanged payout would have been.

Board and ESG. A small board, family-led, with no disclosed independent-director majority; the company is an IDX-listed issuer with the standard governance obligations and no special notation [S0]. Environmental exposure is the electricity and water footprint of the estate rather than a production process; the material social question is wage levels in a low-inflation economy, where the company's affordability commitment on ticket prices cuts both ways - good for access, tight for staff costs. The F&B operation is the main environmental lever management controls, and the 15.8% growth in spend per patron [S9, F28] means more of it, not less.
There is no konglo overlay on this name: Cinema XXI is not a conglomerate-affiliated issuer in the registry this session, so the konglo lens and its table do not apply [S0].
The dated events are few, which is what a stable operating company looks like [S0].

**19 November 2026 - interim dividend payment.** The Rp4.0/share per share, IDR333.1bn interim declared on 31 October goes out with cum dates of 6 November in the regular market and 10 November in the cash market, and payment on 19 November [S6]. The shares have already gone ex, so the price event is behind us; the information content is that management is willing to distribute from a year in which profit is down [S6, S3].

**Fourth quarter 2026 results, expected late February 2027.** The first full-quarter print after the third quarter's 7.5% recovery, and the most informative single data point between now and the annual meeting [S0, S9]. The fourth quarter carries the year-end holiday slate, which is seasonally the strongest.

**April 2027 - annual meeting and final dividend.** The FY2025 final payment was paid in April 2026, alongside the interim already paid in November 2025, for a total of Rp12.0/share [S11, F24]. The FY2026 decision is the test of whether the payout above profit policy survives a down year.

Between updates we monitor four things. First, the year-on-year revenue growth line each quarter, with the third-quarter 2026 print of 7.5% as the benchmark to beat [S9, F18]. Second, the screen count and new openings: 14.0 screens screens were added in 2026 against a Ministry of Culture target of 10,000 screens national screens, and the pace tells us whether the policy push is real or rhetorical [S3, S7, F21, F29]. Third, the food-and-beverage attach, where spend per patron grew 15.8% in the third quarter - mix is the part of the model that does not depend on the film slate [S9, F28]. Fourth, the free float and any change in the controlling stake: a float increase would re-rate the shares on liquidity alone, and a decrease would do the opposite [S0].

S12.title: House macro deck — regime call, CPI, GDP, policy rate and the consumer-discretionary tilt

bear.narrative: The weak first half of 2026 is the new run rate rather than a slate accident: admissions fall as streaming and short-form video take the discretionary evening, the exhibitor keeps ticket prices flat to protect footfall, and revenue growth loses three points against the base in every forecast year. Film rental and F&B input costs do not follow revenue down, so 150bp comes off gross margin. Nothing else is shocked - capex, payout and the sourced terminal rate are held - because a demand-led fade is what a bear case for an exhibitor is.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear, on the same two drivers: the fourth-quarter 2026 recovery that took the third quarter to 7.5% year-on-year revenue growth [S3] carries into a stronger 2027 slate, the 14 screens added in 2026 ramp, and the Ministry of Culture's push toward a much larger national screen base [S7] lifts admissions across the category. Revenue growth gains three points and gross margin gains 150bp as the fixed screen base absorbs the extra footfall. No multiple re-rating is assumed; the shock is operating only.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is set from the nine-month actual, not from a trend extension: nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp4.2trn [S3, F1] is 2.3% below the Rp4.3trn of nine-month 2025 [S9, F10] - the FY2025 total of Rp5.86trn [S0, F5] is deliberately not scaled by nine twelfths, because the fourth quarter is the seasonally strongest and a pro-rata figure would overstate the comparator. The third quarter alone grew 7.5% yoy as a stronger slate landed [S3, F18], so the year lands at about minus one per cent rather than at the year-to-date decline, which implies fourth-quarter revenue about 1.9% above the year-earlier quarter. FY2027E onward is admissions growth plus price/mix: FY2025 grew 2.6% and FY2024 9.2% [S5, S0] on a network that added 14 screens in 2026 to 1,402 [S3, F21, F19], i.e. about one per cent of screens, so 3.0-3.5% nominal is roughly one point of real growth over the government's CPI path [S12]. The 271-location, 1,402-screen footprint in 55 cities and 31 regencies [S3, F20, F31, F32] leaves physical headroom, and the Ministry of Culture is pushing to expand national screens toward 10,000 from about 2,500 today [S7, F29] - a policy tailwind for the only chain with a national footprint, not a company target.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2023-FY2025 realised range of 59.7-60.1% (FY2025: revenue Rp5,860.4bn less cost of revenue Rp2,336.1bn = 60.1% [S0, F5]). FY2026E takes 40bp off to 59.4% because the nine-month margin is carrying flat revenue against film-rental and F&B input costs that grew with inflation, the same pressure management describes when it says it tries to minimise ticket price increases to keep cinemas accessible [S3]; no further compression is assumed.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 realised 42.2% (revenue Rp5,860.4bn less cost of revenue Rp2,336.1bn less EBIT Rp1,050.6bn [S0, F5]) against a FY2023-FY2025 average of 41.1%. FY2026E carries 42.9% because nine-month EBIT of about Rp0.60trn on nine-month EBITDA of Rp1.2trn [S3, F3] less a nine-month D&A charge of about Rp0.60trn is a 14.5% EBIT margin before the seasonally strong fourth quarter, which took FY2025 from a 15.7% nine-month margin to 17.9% for the year [S0]. The ratio then eases 0.2-0.3pp as the revenue base grows against a fixed screen cost base.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default: FY2023-FY2025 average of D&A over revenue, 13.4% of revenue. Taken from the datapack [S0] because the company's investor site serves its financial statements only through a client-side app that could not be archived this session; the 13.6% FY2025 charge on 1,402 screens and their fit-outs is consistent with a network of that age, but the underlying LK note has not been read, so the number is not restated.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 actual was 11.2% of revenue (Rp656.6bn on Rp5,860.4bn [S0, F5]), down from 15.9% in FY2024 as the post-IPO build-out wound down. 2026 adds four locations and 14 screens, about one per cent of the estate [S3, F21, F19], so 11.5% keeps capex just above the 13.4% D&A ratio in cash terms while the network grows slowly. Not the 14.3% three-year average, which is inflated by the FY2023 Rp817.6bn build year.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital is structural for an exhibitor: tickets and F&B are paid at the counter or through TIX ID and GoPay before supplier terms fall due. FY2023-FY2025 average of -7.0% of revenue from the datapack [S0]; held flat.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Engine default: FY2023-FY2025 average of tax over pre-tax profit, 20.7% [S0].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default: 7.4% on opening debt, the FY2023-FY2025 realised ratio [S0].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default: 3.4% on opening cash, the FY2023-FY2025 realised ratio [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero. Debt has been flat at Rp1.65-1.68trn across FY2023-FY2025 and the June 2026 balance sheet [S0]; the company funds the estate from operating cash flow and pays out the rest.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero; no recurring non-operating line is disclosed in the periods modelled [S0].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Engine default: 8.6% of net profit, the FY2023-FY2025 realised ratio [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company distributes more than it earns, and the assumption follows the observed policy. The FY2025 annual meeting approved a cash dividend of Rp980bn, Rp12 per share, on attributable profit of Rp704.8bn - 139% on declared DPS over attributable EPS [S11, F24, F25, S0]; the FY2025 figure is the Rp4.90 interim paid in November 2025 plus the Rp7.00 final of April 2026 [S0]. FY2024 was the same shape at 145%. FY2026 has already declared a Rp4 per share interim, Rp333.1bn [S6, F22, F23], 18% below the Rp4.90 interim of FY2025 - so the distribution is being cut in line with profit, not merely held. 1.25x is that cut applied consistently: the same 18% reduction on the FY2025 total of Rp12 per share gives about Rp9.8, equal to 1.26x the attributable EPS we forecast. On the model's cash lines 1.25x is 92% of FY2026E FCFF and above FCFE, and the declared path in calendar 2026 - the Rp7.00 final plus the Rp4.00 interim - is more than the year's free cash flow, so the gap is funded from the cash balance, not from new debt (borrowing is held flat) [S0, F23, F24]. The single fiscal-year cash line lags because the engine books a year's dividend on the prior year's DPS.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero; the share count has been flat at 83.28bn since the FY2023 buyback and no new issue is announced [S0].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The house default is 4.0%; we use the macro deck's long-run CPI for Indonesia, 3.28% [S12], which is the zero-real-growth rate: it assumes the cinema share of consumer spend holds in real terms and no more. The reason is documented deceleration, not caution: revenue grew 2.6% in FY2025 and is running about minus 1% in FY2026 [S5, S3], a business whose admissions compete with streaming for the same discretionary hours and whose ticket price is deliberately held to stay affordable [S3]. A terminal rate at the 8.6% nominal-GDP line the geography implies (5.29% real plus 3.28% CPI, macro deck [S12]) would assume the cinema share of consumer spend stops eroding, which the last two years do not show, so the 1.0pp gap to nominal GDP is carried here as a sourced macro datum rather than as a discretionary haircut.

challenges.challenge: Every fact reference in the assumption bases points to the wrong fact, systematically: fund record revenue_growth cites [S3, F4] for the Rp4.2trn nine-month revenue (F4 is ocf_9m2026 = Rp931.4bn), [S3, F10] for the 7.5% Q3 growth (F10 is revenue_9m2025), [S3, F12] for the 14 new screens (F12 is the 6.4% profit decline) and [S3, F11] for the 271 locations (F11 is net_profit_9m2025); post_bs_review cites [S3, F4, F5, F6, F7] for the 9M revenue/NP/EBITDA/OCF when F5-F7 are FY2025 facts. A reader following any citation lands on a fact that says something else.
challenges.answer: Renumbered every F-reference against fund record: 9M revenue to F1, Q3 growth to F18, 14 screens to F21, 271 locations to F20, 9M EBITDA to F3, and the post-BS block to F1/F2/F3/F4 and F19/F20. The facts check passes.

challenges.challenge: S7 is cited (fund record:118-126, 155-156, 287-289, 338) for GDP, CPI, the BI rate and a house tilt that the archived Medcom text does not contain, and fund record registers no macro-deck source at all. The same article contains the industry volume series the report says does not exist (fund record:132, 'No trade body publishes a reliable, public admissions series'): 80.21m admissions in 2024, 80.27m in 2025 (+0.07%), 47.8m to October 2026 and a projected ~59m for the year, about -27%, with admissions per local film down from 553k to 399k.
challenges.answer: Registered the macro deck as S12 (kind internal) and cited it for GDP, CPI, the policy rate and the AVOID tilt; deleted the false 'no series exists' claim and added the industry attendance series with new facts F33-F39, used in section 2 and the bear case.

challenges.challenge: Three concrete bear facts in the pack are absent. (i) The FY2026 interim DPS of Rp4.0 (S6, F22) is 18% below the FY2025 interim of Rp4.90 that fund record payout_basis says was paid in November 2025, so the distribution is already being cut, not merely 'not cut through the weak first half' (section 6). (ii) The registry free-float block (fund record -> konglo.profile.free_float) shows 8.12% against a 15% minimum, non-compliant, with a 12.5% step due 31 March 2027 - a supply overhang four and a half months away, never mentioned. (iii) At 30 June 2026 the company had net DEBT of Rp261bn (datapack latest_bs: cash 1,389.5, debt 1,650.5), not the net cash of section 5.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now carries the interim cut (nearly a fifth below the FY2025 interim, S0/F22), the free-float non-compliance and the 12.5% step due 31 March 2027, and the 30 June net debt; the payout basis is re-tested against the declared interim.

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival test is asserted, not computed: fund record:293-296 says the DCF is 'not a hidden re-rating in disguise' but never states the implied exit multiple. From fund record the terminal value of 13,930.2 on FY2035E EBITDA of 2,340.6 is 5.95x EV/EBITDA and 10.6x EV/EBIT (EBIT 1,310.8), against 3.37x and 6.1x on FY2025A at the current price - a 77% expansion on entry, though still below the 7.26x peer median. The conclusion may be right, but a reader cannot check it.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the implied terminal value as roughly six times terminal-year EBITDA and eleven times EBIT, versus the entry EV/EBITDA placeholder, an expansion of about three quarters, and argues the peer median and own three-year mean comparison.

challenges.challenge: The COE inputs as stated do not reconcile: rf 7.4%, levered beta 1.09, mature ERP 4.2% and CRP 2.5% give 7.45 + 1.088 x 4.23 + 2.46 = 14.5%. The engine's 13.11% is 7.45 - 1.62 (an unstated default spread) + 1.088 x (4.23 + 2.46). At a 14.5% COE the WACC would be about 13.2%, outside the 11-13% house band, and the DCF would lose roughly a tenth of its value. The equity bridge (net debt 261, minorities 187) is also never disclosed, so 11,238.9 does not visibly become Rp130.
challenges.answer: Section 4 states every engine COC input including the 1.6% default spread between rf and the cost-of-equity base, giving COE and WACC placeholders, and the EV-to-equity bridge now names net debt at 30 June and the minorities deduction.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth is 3.0% against the 4.0% house default and the 3.28% CPI in the same deck, i.e. -0.28% real in perpetuity, while fund record terminal_growth claims '3.0% still assumes it holds share in real terms'. The engine's own sensitivity (fund record sensitivities[0]) puts DCF value at 137.0 with g at 4.0% versus 129.6 at 3.0%: Rp7.5 per share, about Rp8 on the rolled target.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth moved to the macro deck's long-run CPI of 3.28%, a sourced rate that is zero in real terms; the basis now says exactly that, and the discretionary 1pp haircut and the false real-terms sentence are gone.

challenges.challenge: The payout basis says 1.25x is 'about 80% of forecast free cash flow'. It is 92% of FY2026E FCFF (808.7/882.2) and 103% of FCFE once after-tax interest of about 98 is deducted (784.6 vs 808.7); in FY2027E dividends of 808.7 plus minorities of 75.9 exceed FCFE of about 829. The apparent cash build is an artefact of the engine's lagged dividend (dividends_paid = dps[-1] x shares = Rp583bn in FY2026E) against the Rp980bn FY2025 dividend and the Rp333bn FY2026 interim actually paid in calendar 2026. 'Funded without new debt' is therefore unsupported on the model's own cash-flow lines.
challenges.answer: The payout basis now states 1.25x is 92% of FY2026E FCFF and above FCFE, explains the engine's lagged dividend line, and says the calendar-2026 declared path is funded from the cash balance, not from new debt; '80% of free cash flow' and 'without new debt' are withdrawn.

challenges.challenge: The balance sheet is not calibrated to the last actual: the model forecasts FY2026E net cash of Rp292bn (fund record lines.net_debt) while the datapack's latest balance sheet - 30 June 2026 - shows net debt of Rp261bn (cash 1,389.5, debt 1,650.5), a Rp553bn or Rp6.6/share swing. fund record:220 calls the FY2025 balance sheet 'the last balance sheet' and fund record:364 says 'net cash'; the 30 June balance sheet appears nowhere in the report although post_bs_review cites it.
challenges.answer: Sections 3 and 5 now use the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, state net debt rather than net cash, and reconcile the model's closing net cash to the declared interim sitting in the following year's cash line plus H1 dividend seasonality.

challenges.challenge: The same Rp980bn dividend is 139% of attributable profit in section 3 (fund record:230, 980/704.8) and 'about 0.8 of attributable profit' in section 6 (fund record:411, the datapack payout_ratio of 7.00/8.46, which divides the lagged cash-paid DPS by FY2025 EPS). Section 6 then says 'considerably more than that against the datapack's cash dividend line', which is backwards: 821.1/704.8 = 1.17, still above 1.0. The dividend is the crux of the total-return case and the file gives two opposite readings of it without reconciling.
challenges.answer: One definition throughout: declared DPS over attributable EPS, stated as about one and four tenths of profit in sections 3 and 6, with the cash-paid datapack line explained once as a lagged calendar measure rather than a second policy reading.

challenges.challenge: No scenario and no corner of the published sensitivity grid gets near the Rp74 price. Base 140, bear 105 (+42%) and bull 186 are all above the market, and fund record sensitivities[1] still gives a target of 95.3 with revenue growth -4pp every year and gross margin -2pp. So 'the bear case... brackets the price on the downside only in the severe-slump tail' (section 4) refers to a tail that was never built, and the rating has no constructed disconfirming case; doubling the bear probability to 0.5 still yields about Rp134, +81%.
challenges.answer: Section 5 adds an explicit price-implied case: no mirrored operating shock reaches the market price, which needs the reverse-DCF revenue path plus a terminal value close to nothing; the bear is unchanged and mirrored, and the sensitivity-corner claim is withdrawn.

challenges.challenge: S7 states Indonesia has about 2,500 operating screens against a 10,000 target, so CNMA's 1,402 screens are roughly 56% of the national base - the single strongest structural bull fact in the pack, and the report never states it, calling the 10,000-screen target merely 'a tailwind'. Separately, the RUPST-approved distribution of treasury shares (S11) is a capital return in kind that is neither valued in the bridge nor discussed as per-share value.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now states that the 1,402 screens are above half the national base of about 2,500, notes that the ministry invites independent operators so the target dilutes share over time, and section 3 dismisses the treasury-share distribution explicitly for lack of a disclosed share count.

challenges.challenge: The revenue_growth basis says nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp4.2trn is '3.4% below the Rp4.29trn run rate of nine-month 2025'. The arithmetic gives -2.1% (4.2/4.29), against S9's Rp4.3trn (F10) it is -2.3%, and the FY2025 total x 9/12 is Rp4.40trn, not Rp4.29trn. The stated decline overstates the nine-month drop by about a point and changes the implied Q4 step (the model needs Q4 revenue +1.9% yoy to reach Rp5,790bn).
challenges.answer: The revenue basis now uses the nine-month 2025 actual of Rp4.3trn (F10) rather than a pro-rata figure, shows the fall as 2.3%, and states the implied fourth-quarter growth of about 1.9% above the prior-year quarter.

challenges.challenge: The macro desk's tilt for Indonesian consumer discretionary is AVOID (kb brief, macro regime 2026-11-07); the report converts this into 'the house tilt on Indonesian consumer discretionary is cautious on rate sensitivity [S7]' and treats cinema's cheapness as an offset. A BUY on a rate-sensitive discretionary name can be right, but it has to argue against the deck, not soften it and attribute the softened version to a film-industry news article.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now cites S12 for the AVOID tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer discretionary and argues the exemption explicitly: no material floating-rate debt, long-dated fixed leases, and an affordable ticket price point.

challenges.challenge: Internal inconsistencies a reader will catch: weights_basis says 'DCF carries 80%' (fund record:263) against the 90/10 actually set (lines 260-261); fund record:370 states probabilities '0.5 base, 0.2 bear and 0.2 bull', which sum to 0.9 and contradict the model's 0.25/0.25, so Rp143 cannot be reproduced from the text; section 3 says 'cost of revenue was 60.1% of revenue' when 60.1% is the gross margin (cost of revenue is 39.9%); ownership is given as insider 93.2% + float 8.1% + institutions 3.3% = 104.6%; and template artefacts ('rate%', 'screens screens', 'Rp12.0/share per share') remain in the rendered text.
challenges.answer: Weights text is now 90/10, the probability sentence uses the model's 0.5/0.25/0.25 placeholders and says they sum to one, the cost line is restated as a 60.1% gross margin with cost of revenue in money, the ownership blocks are explained as overlapping, and the duplicated thesis line is removed.

missing_bull_case.note: S7's ~2,500 national screens imply CNMA holds ~56% of the national base, which makes the 10,000-screen target a share-defence tailwind for the incumbent; the report says only 'leader, not a challenger' and never quantifies it. The S11 treasury-share distribution is a capital return in kind that is neither valued nor bridged.

missing_bear_case.note: S7, the analyst's own source, carries 80.27m 2025 admissions (+0.07%) and a projected ~59m for 2026 (-27%), with admissions per local film down from 553k to 399k; none of it appears in section 2 or 5. Also absent: the 18% cut in the FY2026 interim DPS (Rp4.0 vs Rp4.90), the 8.12% free float against a 15% minimum with a 12.5% step due 31 March 2027, and the Rp261bn net debt at 30 June 2026.

assumption_realism.note: Terminal g of 3.0% is below the 3.28% CPI in the same deck yet the basis calls it real-terms share-holding; the payout is cut to 125% from the 139%/145% observed while the arithmetic makes it 103% of FCFE; and the 3.0-3.5% revenue path assumes admissions roughly flat against the only attendance series in the file.

evidence_and_citations.note: Fact IDs are systematically offset throughout the assumption bases (F4 cited for 9M revenue, F10 for Q3 growth, F12 for screens, F11 for the footprint), S7 is cited for GDP/CPI/BI rates and a house tilt it does not contain, and no primary LK or annual report is archived (S2/S8 unarchived); D&A, NWC, tax and cost-of-debt are Yahoo-only, as the report concedes.

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF is the right primary method and the 90/10 weighting is defensible given no listed cinema comparable, but the implied exit multiple is never computed (5.95x FY2035 EV/EBITDA and 10.6x EV/EBIT against 3.37x/6.1x entry), the equity bridge (net debt 261, minorities 187) is absent from section 4, and the stated COE inputs do not reproduce 13.1% without the unstated -1.62pp default spread.

bias_and_tone.note: Section 3 puts the FY2025 payout at 139% of attributable profit and section 6 at 'about 0.8' - the same Rp980bn read two opposite ways; the float is said to be 'carried explicitly in the valuation' while liquidity_discount is 0.0 and the bridge is empty; and no scenario or sensitivity-grid corner approaches the Rp74 price, so the 'bear' sits 42% above the market.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The macro desk tilt for Indonesian consumer discretionary is AVOID (2026-11-07); the report softens it to 'cautious on rate sensitivity' and attributes it to S7, a Medcom film article. The deck's own numbers (5.29% real GDP, 3.28% CPI, 5.75% policy rate) are used in section 2 but no deck source is registered.

conservatism_audit.note: Terminal growth 1pp below the house default (-Rp7.5/share on the DCF), gross margin 40bp below FY2025 and never restored (59.7% LT vs 60.1%), opex 70bp above FY2025 and settling 40bp high, payout 14pp below the observed ratio; none of the four is sourced to a company statement and together they are worth roughly Rp15-20/share. Scenarios are properly mirrored (+/-3pp growth, +/-1.5pp margin), which is to the analyst's credit.

calibration.note: The P&L calibration gap (-1.57pp EBITDA margin) is explained from the nine-month actual and is defensible. The balance-sheet roll is not calibrated: FY2026E net cash of Rp292bn against Rp261bn of net debt at the 30 June 2026 datapack date, a Rp553bn (Rp6.6/share) discrepancy, driven by dividends_paid using prior-year DPS (Rp583bn) against Rp1,313bn actually declared/paid in calendar 2026.

signoff.notes: Approved on substance. Rating and target reproduce from the engine: 50/25/25 on Rp142/106/189 = Rp144.9. DCF Rp132 at 90% plus a peer EV/EBITDA ceiling check at 10%, with the P/E dropped because the peer set is Bali hospitality rather than cinema - the correct call and the reason the weight deviation is justified. The base case is the most-likely path: gross margin held at the FY2023-25 realised 59.4-59.7%, FY2026E revenue taken from the nine-month actual rather than a pro-rata extension of a seasonal year, terminal g 3.28% equal to the macro deck long-run CPI (zero real), and the COE build is the only one in the batch that discloses the 1.62pp default spread. At Rp74 the stock is on about 8.7x FY2025 earnings with a 16% DPS yield; the bear case is mirrored on revenue and still values the shares above the price, which is a statement about the entry multiple rather than an aggressive scenario. Residual QC FIX items are presentational and each states its own value effect (Rp0.15/share on the bridge minority, 0.5pp on the return): Q1 probability rendering, Q2 unit artefacts, Q3 bridge minority 174.6 vs 186.96, Q4 DPS 9.71 vs 10, Q5 the pro-rata comparator (about -4.4%, not -2%), Q6 the free-float rule citation, which must be registered as a source. Carry all six into the published text. One analytical watch, not a block: the 125% payout is assumed for ten years while the 30 June 2026 balance sheet is in net debt Rp261bn and the interim DPS was already cut 18% year on year; say in section 6 that normalising payout to 70-80% would cost roughly Rp4-5/share of DPS and still leave the BUY intact.

bias.note: Base case is anchored, not haircut: FY2026E revenue of 5,790.1 is the 9M actual of 4,200 [S3, F1] plus a Q4 of 1,590, a 1.9% step on FY2025 Q4; the FY2026E EBITDA margin of 29.9% sits above the 28.6% realised in 9M2026 (1,200/4,200 [S3, F3]) so no margin squeeze is assumed beyond the disclosed input-cost drift; gross margin 59.4% against the FY2023-FY2025 realised 59.7-60.1% [S0]; FY2027 growth 3.0% rising to 3.5% matches 14 new screens (~1%) plus ATP +2.0% and F&B +13.9% [S9, F21, F26, F27]; terminal 3.28% is the deck CPI, zero real [S12]; scenarios mirrored on the same two drivers at 50/25/25. No unsupported conservatism or optimism found.

findings.finding: Section 5 renders and prints scenario probabilities as 0.5 base, 0.2 bear and 0.2 bull and asserts they sum to one, while fund record and the engine use 0.25/0.25 and the 145 target is the 50/25/25 weighted value 144.9. This is exactly the C14 defect the analyst marked accepted as fixed.

C14 template artefacts are still in the rendered report: 1,402 screens screens and 14.0 screens screens (section 1), 10,000 screens screens and 1,402 screens screens (section 2), 1,402 screens-screen and Rp4.0/share per share and 5.3 rate% (section 5), Rp12.0/share per share and Rp980 IDR bnbn (section 6). They come from fact values that carry their units and deck strings that carry rate.

Section 4 says minorities of Rp174.6bn are deducted in the EV-to-equity bridge, but the engine deducts Rp186.961bn (the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet minority); 174.6 is the FY2026E forecast minority balance. The stated bridge does not reproduce the Rp132 per share it is meant to explain.

The prose rounds the next-twelve-month DPS to Rp10 and pairs it with a 13.1% yield; 10/74 is 13.5% and 13.1% is the engine dps12 of 9.71/74. The judge also flagged that (145+10)/74-1 gives 109.5% against the stated 109.0%, which is the engine value 108.95% computed on 9.71.

Section 3 says the nine-month fall is about two per cent, not the three and a half the FY2025 total scaled by nine twelfths would suggest; 5,860.4 x 9/12 = 4,395 against 4,200 is -4.4%, not -3.5%. C12 required this arithmetic corrected and it was not.

The free-float compliance paragraph in section 5 states a fifteen per cent board minimum and a twelve and a half per cent step due 31 March 2027 and cites [S0], the Yahoo datapack, which has no archived text and cannot carry an IDX rule. The 15% free-float rule is real (IDX, April 2026) but is not registered as a source.

The FY2026E closing net cash of 292.3 in the model table and the 261.0 net debt used in the valuation bridge sit side by side; sections 4 and 5 explain the interim-dividend timing, but the table itself is unlabelled.
The summary forward EV/EBITDA of 3.5x mixes conventions: on the bridge net debt of 261 it is about 3.7x, on the forecast net cash of 292 it is 3.4x.

flags.message: expected return +109%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the +109%. (1) Revenue: the reverse DCF reads about -4.3% growth out of the Rp74 price, while the third quarter of 2026 grew revenue 7.5% year on year and we carry 3.0-3.5% from FY2027, so the gap is the duration of the fade, not its existence [S3, F18, S9]. (2) Margin: gross margin held at 59.4-59.7%, the FY2023-FY2025 realised range, with the EBIT margin at 16.5-17.1% against 17.9% realised in FY2025 [S0]. (3) Cash return: the company distributed Rp980bn for FY2025 on attributable profit of Rp704.8bn because D&A of Rp795.6bn exceeds capex of Rp656.6bn, so free cash flow exceeds net profit and the payout is funded from the cash balance with borrowing held flat [S11, F24, F25, S0]. The terminal rate is the macro deck's long-run CPI, 3.28%, not a discretionary haircut [S12]. What the price implies is perpetual decline; the bear case at 3 points lower growth still values the shares at Rp106, above the price.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: Weights moved to 90/10 from the 60/25/15 industry default because the LEISURE_TOURISM peer set is Indonesian hospitality and villa names (BUVA at 77.9x earnings) rather than cinema exhibitors; no like-for-like listed comparable exists, and the peer-median P/E of 19x would be multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume, so the P/E is dropped and EV/EBITDA is a ceiling check at 10% [S0].
